title: More Than Half of Americans Worry About AI's Impact on the Environment
summary: Have you ever asked a chatbot a question? That answer might come from a giant building called a data center — and those buildings use a LOT of electricity and water. A new poll from The Associated Press, NORC, and the University of Chicago found that 53% of Americans are 'extremely' or 'very' concerned about AI's impact on the environment. That's up from 41% last year. More than half worry that data centers will raise electricity prices and strain water supplies in nearby towns. 'We're undertaking a massive experiment in real time, and I don't think there'll be any putting the milk back in the bottle,' said Michael Greenstone, who directs the University of Chicago institute that helped with the survey. Data centers aren't the biggest water users in the country, but they can be a big deal locally. 'There's a lot of water usage by AI data centers that's taking away from other things like agriculture and farmers,' said Gedeon Kebede, a computer science student from Cincinnati. President Donald Trump has urged communities to welcome the facilities, saying they bring jobs. But some people, like Nancy Antunes, a retired Democrat from Massachusetts, feel decisions are made for companies, not communities. The debate is heating up as more data centers are built across the U.S.
why_it_matters: The apps and chatbots kids use every day are run by real machines in real towns, and the power and water they use can affect what families pay and what farmers can grow.

background_read: The numbers in the article come from a poll by The Associated Press (a big American news company that gathers news from around the world), NORC (a research group at the University of Chicago that runs surveys), and the university.
AI has grown very fast in the last few years, and companies keep building new data centers packed with powerful computers — those computers need both electricity and water to keep cool.
Data centers are not the country's biggest water users overall, but in one town they can use a lot, which is why neighbors sometimes argue about them.
Article_Structure: WHO: 53% of Americans surveyed by The Associated Press, NORC, and the University of Chicago, plus experts and neighbors like Michael Greenstone and Nancy Antunes.
WHAT: More than half of Americans are 'extremely' or 'very' concerned about AI's effect on the environment, up from 41% a year ago.
WHERE: Across the United States, especially in towns where new data centers are being built.
WHY: Data centers use lots of electricity and water, and people disagree about whether the jobs they bring are worth the strain on local power and water supplies.

perspectives.description: People like Nancy Antunes feel decisions are made for companies, not for the communities that live near the data centers.
President Donald Trump and others say communities should welcome the buildings because they bring jobs.
Experts like Michael Greenstone say this is a giant experiment happening right now, and once it starts it will be hard to undo.
